questions.q: What is Snowflake's full object hierarchy, from top to bottom, per this lesson?
options: Organization → Account → Database → Schema → Object
Account → Organization → Schema → Database → Object
Database → Account → Schema → Object → Organization
Organization → Schema → Account → Database → Object
questions.explain: Every object is namespaced through this chain: organization, then account, then database, then schema, then the object itself (a table, view, or governance object).

questions.q: In the SQL example, what does `USE DATABASE governance_demo; USE SCHEMA sales;` accomplish?
options: It deletes the database and schema
It sets the session's working context so unqualified object names resolve against governance_demo.sales
It grants privileges on the database to the current role
It creates the database and schema
questions.explain: USE DATABASE/USE SCHEMA set context for the session — they don't create or grant anything, they just point unqualified references at that database/schema.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the database/schema hierarchy matters specifically for governance, not just for organizing tables?
options: Because masking policies, row access policies, and tags are ordinary schema objects, and privileges are grantable at every level of the hierarchy
Because Snowflake requires all governance objects to live in a database named GOVERNANCE
Because schemas automatically encrypt all data inside them
Because the hierarchy has no real effect on governance, it's purely cosmetic
questions.explain: Governance objects (masking policies, row access policies, tags) are created inside schemas just like tables, and privileges can be scoped at the database, schema, or individual-object level — which is exactly why understanding this hierarchy is a prerequisite for RBAC.

questions.q: Which statement lists every schema inside a specific database?
options: SHOW DATABASES;
SHOW SCHEMAS IN DATABASE governance_demo;
SHOW TABLES IN SCHEMA governance_demo.sales;
SELECT CURRENT_SCHEMA();
questions.explain: SHOW SCHEMAS IN DATABASE <name> walks one level of the hierarchy — the schemas inside that specific database.

questions.q: What does a fully qualified object name like `governance_demo.sales.orders` represent?
options: A column named orders inside a table named sales
The object orders, inside schema sales, inside database governance_demo
A random alias with no structural meaning
A role hierarchy path
questions.explain: Fully qualified names follow database.schema.object — this uniquely identifies any object in the account, independent of session context.
